title: Love a show that knows what’s necessary to tell the story and what is...
transcript: It seems the theater discourse do sure is the colorblind casting of the notebook musical on Broadway. One thing I specifically wanted to talk about is the fact that this is not the first time a show has done this. When we think of colorblind casting, I think a lot of people immediately think of the Brandy Cinderella as like this. This is our family, and we don't care, and the races don't matter. But, of course, what makes the notebook unique is that you have multiple races of people playing the same character in the same show. That, however, is not unique to just the notebook. A couple years ago, I saw the world premiere of a new musical, Rattlesnake Kate, that was actually about a real person who lived. And that real person and the time period that she lived in would have been treated very differently if she was not actually a white woman. Despite that, however, in the musical adaptation, she was played by three different women, and all three of them were different races. You had the younger version, who is an Asian woman, the middle version, who is white woman, and the older version, who is a black woman. And in that story specifically, it worked because even though in real life she would have been treated differently, the story that they were trying to tell on that stage was specifically about the treatment of women in general. In some of the common experiences. That just women face, and so having that be portrayed by different women who are different body types, different races, different ages, really worked for that production. Because of the direction of the show and the design of the show, people weren't ever confused about who that character was. It was very clear that they were all playing Kate. Another example of colorblind casting is frozen, and not even just on Broadway and the tour, but also live at the Hyperion at Disneyland. This is a show that has consistently been cast colorblind, and that includes the young versions of both Elsa and Anna. So I have seen it multiple times where young Elsa and Anna were different races than older Elsa and Anna, and the kids that were in the audience not care or did not notice. And frankly, I didn't either, because ultimately, at the end of the day, we all knew that those were Elsa and Anna, both younger and grown up, and the races were not important to the story. Now, I do think that there are plenty of instances of shows that should be cast color consciously rather than being cast colorblind. These are usually very realistic shows. Or the show and what it's trying to say, the context of that changes drastically when the person playing the role is a different race. I think of things like death of a salesman, where the lot of the aspects of that show change drastically when you Had an all black family as opposed to having an all white Loman family. Notebook, on the other hand, specifically the stage version, is just a love story of, like, who were destined to love. There is definitely conflict in the story, but like, all of it is class based. While the film and the novel are set in a time and place where the races of both Noah and Ali would greatly affect the outcome of that story, specifically in the stage version, they take all of that out. So it could basically be set anywhere, anytime, any place. Well, at least a time and place without cell phones, because cell phones would greatly affect the entire outcome of the story of the notebook, even more so than their race. Sure, it does require some suspension of disbelief to believe that Jordan, Tyson, Mary, and Puckett are playing the same character on that stage. But that would have to take place no matter whether they were the same race or not. No matter what, there's still two different women playing the same character. Which to me, is no different than believing that there is a full house on that stage, despite the fact that it is very much a set piece. If this were at all a realistic story that is being told in a specific time, a specific place where race would change the outcome, then I think, yeah, we need to talk about color conscious casting. But In the case of this production and the story that's being told here, for me personally, it just doesn't matter.
